weeks.title: Responsible ML — Fairness, Privacy, Explainability
weeks.context:
Machine learning systems can harm people. Not through dramatic AI takeover scenarios, but through mundane mechanisms: a hiring algorithm that systematically disadvantages one demographic group, a lending model that charges higher rates to historically redlined communities, a medical diagnosis model that performs worse on underrepresented groups. These harms are not hypothetical — they have occurred in deployed systems. Responsible ML is the set of practices that reduce the likelihood and severity of these harms.

Fairness in ML is not a single concept — it is a family of definitions that are mathematically incompatible with each other in most non-trivial cases. Demographic parity requires equal positive prediction rates across groups. Equalised odds requires equal true positive and false positive rates across groups. Calibration requires that predicted probabilities match actual outcome rates for each group. A model cannot satisfy all three simultaneously when base rates differ between groups. This is the fundamental fairness impossibility theorem, and it forces you to make explicit value judgments about which definition fits your use case.

Measuring bias starts with disaggregated metrics: compute accuracy, precision, recall, and false positive rate separately for each protected group in your dataset. If your flight delay model has 78% accuracy for domestic flights but 61% accuracy for international flights, that is a performance disparity that requires investigation regardless of whether the groups are legally protected. Disaggregated evaluation is the baseline practice that every ML project should perform.

Mitigation falls into three categories: pre-processing (reweight or resample training data to reduce representation imbalances), in-processing (add fairness constraints to the training objective), and post-processing (adjust prediction thresholds separately for each group to equalise a chosen metric). Each approach has tradeoffs in complexity, accuracy cost, and which fairness definition it optimises.

Differential privacy adds mathematical guarantees about individual privacy in model training. An epsilon-differentially private model provides a formal bound on how much any individual's data can affect the model's outputs, limiting the information that can be extracted about training set members.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You compute demographic parity for your loan model across income quintiles. The lowest income quintile is approved at a 15% rate while the highest income quintile is approved at a 62% rate. Is this a fairness problem? The answer requires context. If the base rate of loan repayment (the ground truth) differs across income quintiles in the same proportion, then a model with demographic disparity in approvals may actually be calibrated — it is reflecting the true difference in repayment probability. If the model's approval rate differs more than the base rate difference, it is adding disparity beyond what the underlying data supports. Always compare approval rate disparity to ground truth base rate disparity. Disparity greater than the base rate difference is evidence of algorithmic unfairness.

weeks.title: Capstone — A Full ML System, Shipped
weeks.context:
The capstone is where everything comes together: a full ML system, designed, built, monitored, and shipped. Not just a model. A system — with a data pipeline, a training pipeline, a serving endpoint, monitoring, reproducibility, and documentation. The combination of all these pieces, working together reliably, is what ML engineering produces.

The scoping decision is the hardest part. The instinct is to build something impressive — distributed training, multimodal inputs, real-time monitoring. The right instinct is to build something that works end-to-end with all the engineering quality that implies. A clean, well-monitored, reproducible logistic regression pipeline is a stronger capstone than a messy deep learning system with no monitoring and non-reproducible training.

End-to-end thinking means designing the data pipeline, model, serving, and monitoring as one integrated system before writing any code. Where does the data come from? How does it get preprocessed? Where are the preprocessing artifacts stored so inference uses the same transformations as training? How does the serving endpoint load the model? What metrics does the monitoring collect? What triggers a retraining run? Writing a one-page system design before writing code is the difference between building a system and building a collection of scripts.

The retrospective is as important as the technical work. What decisions turned out to be wrong? What would you architect differently? What took five times longer than expected and why? What would be the first thing to improve in v2? An honest retrospective shows engineering maturity. It demonstrates that you understand the tradeoffs you made, not just the system you built.

Ship something, monitor it, and tell the story. The deliverables: a live endpoint with a public URL, a SYSTEM-DESIGN.md that describes the architecture, an eval report with honest metrics, a monitoring dashboard showing recent predictions, and a retrospective document. The story: a 3-minute demo video and a write-up that explains what problem you solved and why the engineering decisions you made were the right ones.
